FEMA's cost-sharing rewards risk and waste. Real reform means shifting disaster costs to states and the private sector, where incentives align with risk, argues Cato’s @LettDominik.

What if you could design your own job—and get paid to do it? The Cato Innovation Project creates two-year paid positions at the Cato Institute.  

🔹 You design and propose your own full-time paid job to advance the principles of individual liberty, limited government, free markets, and peace.  

🔹 Cato decides whether to fund it by hiring you.  

Apply now: ow.ly/QRFk50YXJRt

School choice is spreading fast. But launching a program is only the first step. Without the right design, families face wait lists, red tape, and lost opportunities. Cato's @ColleenHroncich lays out the best practices that make school choice work.

ow.ly/EsW050YXR9C

The House voted 235–191 to reauthorize Section 702 mass surveillance with a no warrant requirement for searching Americans' communications. The Fourth Amendment contains no national security exception—and 18 years of abuses prove why it shouldn’t, explains Cato’s Patrick Eddington

ow.ly/MtFe50YXM0q

The Pentagon’s retaliation campaign against Senator Kelly is unconstitutional, explain Cato’s scholars.

Cato’s amicus brief explains why punishing Kelly’s speech is impermissible.

ow.ly/lHF750YXNfZ

Regulators said they ended “reputational risk” rules—but an exemption says otherwise. If controversy can be framed as a financial risk, banks can still be pushed to drop lawful clients. Congress should remove this possibility for good, says Cato’s Norbert J. Michel and Nicholas Anthony. 

ow.ly/5PcE50YXFTc

How can America unleash the next energy revolution?

On May 13, the Cato Institute will host Secretary of Energy @SecretaryWright to discuss the current state of energy policy — and what's to come.

Register: ow.ly/2Sru50YXFwh

The Trump administration’s Jones Act waiver is revealing what protectionism hides: suppressed demand for American coastal shipping, natural US trade lanes blocked by law, and allies—not adversaries—stepping up. It’s time for permanent reform, says Cato’s @scottlincicome.
ow.ly/YSam50YWG7e
Good intentions don't make good policy—results do. A reminder from Milton Friedman that government initiatives should be judged by what they deliver, not how they sound.

The recent hantavirus cluster is a reminder that infectious disease does not stop at borders. But the World Health Organization’s failures during Covid — and its mission drift beyond core disease surveillance — show that global cooperation is only as good as the institutions built to deliver it. 

On the latest Cato Podcast, @MrRBourne talks with @RogerBate3 about what a narrower, more accountable model of international health cooperation would look like.

Listen to it on Apple, Spotify, and our

For years, Cato scholars have warned that successive administrations of both parties have stretched emergency trade statutes far beyond what Congress intended.

The Constitution vests the power to lay and collect duties squarely in Congress.

ow.ly/Vcvi50YWLQ5

Federal farm subsidies have kept growing from occasional disaster relief into a sprawling system of commodity supports, crop insurance, sugar protection, and bailouts. With the backdrop of the Farm Bill, Cato’s @MrRBourne, @catoedwards, and @clark_packard discuss who really benefits, why reform never sticks, and how tariffs hurt farmers that Congress then subsidizes.

Listen on Apple, Spotify, and our website.

FDA oversight can prevent harms—but also blocks patient access. Jeffrey A. Singer says federal gatekeeping isn’t the only path to safety, especially for patients with treatment‑resistant depression/PTSD. A better way involves informing patients and physicians, and allowing choice.

ow.ly/2hMN50YWeiR

The trade court ruling against President Trump’s Section 122 tariffs is a victory for the rule of law—but the tariff saga continues, explains Cato’s @AlfredCObregon.

Video

Cato University brings together college and graduate students to study the principles of liberty and their real-world policy applications. Participants connect with top scholars, receive free resources and travel stipends, and join a growing network of future leaders.

Video

The court ruled that Section 122 tariffs were unlawful, but the practical impact is limited, says Cato’s Alfredo Carrillo Obregon. These tariffs were intended as a temporary stopgap between the IEEPA tariffs and future tariffs imposed under other executive powers. More tariff announcements are likely in the coming months.

The Founders knew slavery clashed with the liberty they proclaimed—and many said so plainly. Timothy Sandefur revisits Dunmore’s Proclamation, Jefferson’s “tremble” line, and a little-known 1769 freedom case that complicates the “hypocrisy” story.

ow.ly/xV1c50YW2rP
The trade court’s ruling against President Trump’s Section 122 tariffs is a victory for the rule of law and the separation of powers, says Cato Institute’s @clark_packard.

Banning minors from “companion” AI chatbots may feel protective—but the evidence is mixed, and the unintended costs could be real. Many teens can’t access therapy; surveys find chatbots are often helpful, and some users report they prevented suicide. Policy should weigh both sides.
